newsitem.title: UK: Aluminium moves up but cautious over Russian news.
newsitem.headline: Aluminium moves up but cautious over Russian news.

text.p: Aluminium prices pushed higher during Friday afternoon London Metal Exchange (LME) trading, as news emerged that some Russian aluminium smelters were considering cutting production, traders said.
LME three months prices were trading at $1,335 a tonne, up from levels of $1,324 prior to the news, but little different from Thursday, with traders adopting caution.

In Moscow, Oleg Deripaska, chief executive officer of Sayansk Aluminium said he expected a decision to decrease production at Bratsk, Sayansk and Krasnoyarsk after the Kontsern Aluminy producers' group meets.
Western experts and officials adopted a wait-and-see attitude to the possible development.
"These guys (Russians) have the highest production costs in the world," said Tony Bird of industry specialists Anthony Bird and Associates.
Current capacity at Bratsk, Krasnoyarsk, and Sayansk is 850,000, 810,000, and 270,000 tonnes respectively, he noted.
But although Russian smelters do have high costs, they are able to shrug them off by simply not paying bills for power and some materials, he noted.
And some of these plants are located in remote Siberia, where shutting down production facilities and laying off workers is not an option.
Also in Moscow, a Canadian diplomat said Russian and Canadian government officials had recently met to discuss curbing Russian output.
Traders said this re-awakened memories of the Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) between major producers Russia, Australia, Canada, the European Union, Norway and the United States.
The MOU ran from early 1994, expiring earlier this year, and was designed to reduce output by 10 percent and draw down bloated inventories.

"I have not heard anything along those lines...But in the original MOU the Russians are widely believed to have just stockpiled the metal they said they were cutting, and this is now being exported," Bird said.

Officials at the International Primary Aluminium Institute (IPAI), who monitored production levels during the MOU, said discussions recently had focused on maintaining statistical links between the signatories.
"I am not aware of any new initiative or any new talks," an IPAI official said.
